label: Self-heating materials
summary: Some materials heat themselves until they catch fire: rags, steel wool or sanding dust wet with linseed oil or stain; damp hay; pool shock that gets wet or oily; and wet quicklime. Heat builds inside the pile, so rags can smoulder for hours before flames show, and hay can ignite weeks after baling.
signs: Rags, steel wool or sanding dust used with linseed or teak oil, oil-based paint or stain, varnish or polyurethane, above all when bunched up or piled
Cans whose label says DANGER OF COMBUSTION, or that rags used with the product may begin to burn by themselves
Rags soaked in cooking or fish oil too: rapeseed, corn, peanut and safflower oil can self-heat like linseed, while mineral oils such as lubricating oil are not prone to it
Hay baled damp (over about 20% moisture) or wetted in storage, mostly in the first 6 weeks. Hot hay smells of caramel, tobacco or burning, or strongly musty, gives off steam or smoke, or feels hot
Big compost, mulch, manure and leaf piles, and laundry piled up while still hot
Pool shock (calcium hypochlorite) that has got damp, or sits near oil, grease, sawdust, rags or other pool chemicals
Torn or wet bags of quicklime (calcium oxide): with water it gets hot enough to light paper, wood or cloth
do: Lay oily rags out flat in a single layer, outdoors on concrete, away from anything that burns and out of direct sun, with the corners weighed down, until completely dry
Or put them, and oily steel wool and sanding dust, straight into a metal can, fill it with water, close the lid tight and keep it away from buildings
Keep compost, mulch, manure and leaf piles small and away from buildings so the heat can escape
Bale hay dry: under about 22% moisture for small square bales and 18% for large bales. Check damp-baled stacks twice a day for 6 weeks with a long pipe probe and a thermometer

Hay at about 65 °C (150 °F) will likely keep climbing: move the bales apart to cool and check every 2 hours. At about 80 °C (175 °F) fire is imminent or already burning inside: stop moving the hay, which feeds the fire
Store pool shock dry, off the floor and apart from other pool chemicals, acids, oil, grease, rags and sawdust; even a wet scoop put back in the pail can start a reaction
Keep quicklime in dry, closed containers, away from paper, wood, cloth and anything damp
dont: Don't leave oily rags scrunched up or piled, even outdoors: the pile holds the heat in, and the bigger the pile and the warmer the day, the greater the risk

Don't walk straight onto a hay stack that may be hot: burned-out hollows can collapse under you. Walk on boards or a ladder laid across it, work in pairs, and wear a rope held by someone off the stack

Don't pull apart hay, compost or other piles that are smoking or very hot: fresh air can make them burst into flame. If fuel, fertiliser or pesticide is stored nearby, leave it and go; if not, get animals out, cut a 4.5 m (15 ft) firebreak round an outdoor stack, wet roofs downwind
Don't let water, oil or other chemicals into pool shock, and don't use a dry-chemical (ABC) or CO2 extinguisher on it: flood a pool-chemical fire with lots of water from a distance
Don't put water on quicklime or use it on a fire involving quicklime: it reacts violently with water, giving off heat, and its maker says not to use water and lists dry chemical as the extinguisher
Don't close up a pool-chemical container that has started to react: pressure can build up inside
ppe: Indirect-vent goggles and chemical-resistant gloves for quicklime and pool shock: wet lime burns skin and causes serious eye damage
A particulate respirator such as an N95 for lime dust where the air doesn't move much
firstAid: Lime or pool chemical in an eye: rinse with clean water for at least 15 minutes, taking out contact lenses, then get medical help
On skin: brush off dry lime or powder first, take off contaminated clothing, then wash with plenty of water for 15 to 20 minutes; get medical help for burns or irritation that doesn't settle
Breathed lime dust or chlorine fumes: get to fresh air and rest. Chlorine can cause fluid in the lungs hours later, so keep watching them for 48 hours; for coughing or a tight chest, see Chemicals
Burns from a smouldering pile: cool under cool running water for 20 minutes and cover with cling film or a clean cloth; see Hot surfaces
